contributions: AutoL2S, a distillation framework where the model jointly generates a lightweight switching token (<EASY>) as part of its own output, enabling implicit, instance-wise selection between long and short verified reasoning paths without explicit length constraints

a GRPO-style second training stage that uses the SFT model's own induced long-short rollouts (rather than externally imposed length targets) to correct residual length-accuracy misalignment while preserving the base long-CoT capability

up to 71.7% reasoning-length reduction with negligible accuracy loss across six reasoning benchmarks and two backbones, outperforming five state-of-the-art efficient-reasoning baselines (O1-Pruner, CoT-Valve, DPO, TokenSkip, AlphaOne) on the accuracy-length trade-off

an attention-pattern and information-theoretic analysis showing why concatenated long-then-short training (rather than separate long/short training) produces more reliable short-path behavior -- long CoT paths supply auxiliary information that stabilizes short-path learning early in training
limitations: AutoL2S's performance depends on the availability and quality of paired long and short reasoning annotations, which the authors note may be costly to obtain for some domains. The binary long/short distinction may not fully capture more fine-grained variations in reasoning complexity that a continuous or multi-level length control might better address. Efficiency measurements focus on autoregressive decoding settings; gains may differ under alternative inference paradigms (e.g. batched/speculative decoding). The authors' ethics statement flags that improved reasoning efficiency could lower deployment costs for models without addressing existing limitations like hallucination, bias, and unreliability, so efficiency gains should not be read as a general safety improvement.
method: Two-stage training. Stage 1 (SFT): builds a dataset pairing each question with a verified long CoT (from a strong teacher, DeepSeek-R1, distilled via Bespoke-Stratos-17k) and, where obtainable, a verified short CoT (generated by a weaker short-CoT teacher, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, via rejection sampling with k trials, keeping the shortest correct candidate); questions with a valid short CoT are annotated with a lightweight <EASY> switching token prepended before a <Short Trigger>, while questions without one retain only the long path. The model is trained to jointly generate the <EASY>/<Long Trigger> decision as part of its own output sequence, so long-short mode selection is learned implicitly with no explicit length constraint or classifier. Stage 2 (RL): uses the SFT model's own long-short rollouts (induced by forcing <Long Trigger> vs. <Short Trigger>) in a GRPO-style objective with a correctness-based advantage (reward 1 if the rollout reaches the correct answer, 0 otherwise) and a clipped importance-sampling ratio keeping the policy close to the SFT model -- this reinforces correct outcomes under whichever length was already selected, correcting residual length-accuracy misalignment left by the SFT stage without directly penalizing length. Evaluated on Llama3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbones across six benchmarks (Math500, GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K, OlympiadBench-Math, AIME24, MMLU-Pro) against five baselines (Bespoke-Stratos R1-distilled models, O1-Pruner, CoT-Valve, DPO, TokenSkip, AlphaOne).
one_liner: AutoL2S distills non-reasoning LLMs into models that jointly generate a lightweight <EASY> switching token and correspondingly select long or short chain-of-thought paths per instance, then refines this with GRPO-style RL on the induced long-short rollouts, cutting reasoning length by up to 71.7% with negligible accuracy loss across six benchmarks.
problem: Reasoning distillation trains student LLMs to imitate full long-form teacher reasoning uniformly across all inputs, treating long reasoning as necessary even for simple questions and causing overthinking (excessive CoT length, high inference cost); naively shortening reasoning globally degrades accuracy because reasoning length has no unique ground-truth label -- for many inputs, multiple reasoning paths of different lengths reach correct answers, and whether concise reasoning suffices is often only observable through outcome correctness, so effective compression must be an instance-wise decision rather than uniform truncation.

relevance.overthinking: Core paper for this topic: explicitly names 'overthinking' as the problem distillation introduces and directly targets the archive's central accuracy/efficiency tradeoff question. Its explicit argument that reasoning length has no unique ground-truth label -- multiple correct paths of different lengths can exist for the same input -- and that this necessitates instance-wise rather than uniform-truncation compression is a clean articulation of the theoretical challenge underlying much of this archive's length-control literature, and its Force-Short/Force-Long ablation is direct, controlled evidence that neither extreme (always-short, always-long) matches an instance-adaptive policy.

results: AutoL2S achieves the best average accuracy-length trade-off among all compared methods on both backbones, compressing reasoning paths by up to 71.7% relative to the strong Bespoke-Stratos distilled baseline with negligible accuracy degradation (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: average accuracy 0.573 vs. Bespoke-Stratos-7B's 0.590, a 1.7-point drop, at 2103 average tokens vs. 6748 -- a 71.7% length reduction). On several individual benchmarks AutoL2S actually improves accuracy over the long-only baseline while still shortening reasoning substantially. Rejection sampling in the SFT stage matters: disabling it (k=0, 'w/o RJ') degrades RL rollout quality; using k=8 yields the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with relative token-length improvements of ~71% (3B) and ~53% (7B) versus weaker rejection-sampling settings. An SFT-only ablation (AutoL2S-SFT) confirms the RL stage adds further gains: the full AutoL2S consistently beats AutoL2S-SFT on the accuracy-length trade-off. Forcing the model to always use short reasoning ('w/ Force-Short') or always long ('w/ Force-Long') both underperform AutoL2S's own adaptive routing decision -- uniformly enforcing short reasoning introduces noisy training signal (aimlessly truncated paths can remove necessary intermediate steps), while forced-long uses ~15% more tokens for similar accuracy -- confirming the value of the model's own instance-wise <EASY> decision over either extreme. An annotation-format ablation shows 'Long-Short Distill' (long CoT concatenated before short CoT in training) beats 'Short-Long Distill' and separately-constructed variants, and an attention-map analysis across training steps shows long CoT reasoning paths significantly shape the attention patterns learned for short CoT generation early in training, with the correlation diminishing later as the two modes become distinct learned behaviors -- offered as a mechanistic explanation (paired with an information-theoretic argument, Lemma 1 in the appendix) for why pairing long and short paths in training, rather than training them separately, produces more reliable short-path behavior.
